data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The apparent resilience advantage of decentralized networks is an observer bias artifact: extreme value statistics ensure that the shared cause capable of synchronizing independent operators is discovered only after catastrophic failure, making independence unfalsifiable.","counterconditions":[{"case":"We can identify, in advance, a complete enumeration of shared causes and observe that decentralized operators do not share any of them","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The observation window is long enough to capture multiple rare shared-cause events and the network remains uncorrelated","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The shared cause is genuinely novel and could not have been enumerated in advance, making the reclassification principled rather than post hoc","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"For any finite observation window, decentralized operators appear uncorrelated because the shared cause (e.g., a specific upstream provider failure, a TLS certificate expiry, or a DNS outage) has not yet occurred. When it does occur, the failure is retrospectively reclassified as correlated. This is an extreme value statistics problem: the rare shared cause exists from the start but is below detection threshold until it triggers. The claim 'independent until a shared cause is found' is unfalsifiable because the shared cause can always be found post hoc, making the superiority of decentralization an artifact of observation window rather than a structural property.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
